extracted.intended_audience: scholars/readers of early modern English literature; bibliographers and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive commentary on composing and presenting short character sketches ('characters' / essays) in early 17th-century English—what they represent, tone, and authorial expectations. Includes notes about titles, purpose, sources, and stylistic qualities valued by contemporaries and later critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should represent diverse professions/types
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are intended to represent 'divers severall professions' and various social types (e.g., the world, an old man, a woman, a plowman, a scholar, a tinker, Bridewell, Newgate, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'representing to the eye of the minde divers severall professions' (Saltonstall). The volumes list many specific archetypes (see lists of 'Original Characters' and additions), implying that a good collection should include a variety of social roles and public places so readers can recognise types across society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a title carefully (titles are first judged)
rubrics_metrics.description: The title is the first leaf that comes under censure; readers may dislike a name for the work and judge by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'The title is the first leafe that cometh under censure, some, perhaps, will dislike the name of pictures.' Advice implies authors should be mindful of the title's impact on reception and clarity of genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable opacity: characters need not be perfectly smooth; leave knots for readers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the nature of a character to be perfectly smooth; acceptable to have some 'fast and loose knots' that the ingenious reader may untie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'it is not the nature of a character, to be as smooth as a bull-rush, but to have some fast and loose knots, which the ingenious reader may easily untie.' This counsels allowing some ambiguity or roughness in sketches rather than over-polished, fully-explicit exposition—trusting readers to interpret and resolve details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters can serve moral/pedagogic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Character sketches may be designed to instruct readers morally—e.g., the description of a maid is offered so 'young men may read, and from thence learn that vertue is the truest beauty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'The first picture is the description of a maide, which young men may read, and from thence learn to know, that vertue is the truest beauty.' Authors may intentionally craft sketches as exempla to teach or reinforce moral lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intended tone: recreation rather than ostentation of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The essays/characters are written to recreate (amuse/occupy leisure) rather than to seek fame or scholarly credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing from the dedication: 'Ocium magis foventes, quam studentes gloriae, as sheapheards play upon their oaten pipes, to recreate themselves, not to get credit.' Guidance: aim for a pleasing, recreational tone suited to fireside or leisure reading rather than lofty scholarly display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground characters in personal experience for credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters and essays drawn from an author's own experience ('Probatum est') are presented as more trustworthy and appropriate material for depiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Geffray Mynshul's dedication: 'I gathered a handfull of essayes, and few characters of such things as by my owne experience I could say Probatum est.' This implies a criterion of verisimilitude—use observed experience to inform sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and ease of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary and later critics praise simplicity and an easy, elegant style as a positive quality in such prose and verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example appraisal: Nicholas Breton's poetical powers were 'distinguished by a simplicity, at once easy and elegant.' Guidance: prefer clarity and graceful simplicity over ornate complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine ironic tone with instructive intent where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Collections are described as 'Ironical and Instructive,' indicating that irony/satire paired with corrective or instructive aims is a recognized mode for characters/essays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title example: 'Essayes and Characters, Ironical and Instructive.' Guidance: authors may use irony and satire to expose faults while still teaching or instructing readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange pieces for seasonal/leisure reading and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The material is explicitly intended to be read at leisure ('in winter you may reade them ad ignem, by the fire-side, and in summer ad umbram, under some shadie tree'), suggesting arrangement and length suited to casual reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original phrasing: 'set together in this little book, that in winter you may reade them ad ignem ... and therewith passe away the tedious howres.' Guidance: format and pacing should suit short sittings and accessibility to general readers.
